tips.title: Apply the definition, not the feeling
tips.body: **Renewable means replenished as it is used** — not clean, not unlimited. That is why **bio-fuel is renewable** despite burning, and **nuclear is not** despite producing no carbon dioxide.

tips.title: Nuclear fuel fits neither box
tips.body: It is **not renewable**, because uranium is finite. And it is **not a fossil fuel**, because it is not the remains of living things and is not burned. Being able to say what it is *not*, twice, is what questions test.

tips.title: Predictable is not constant
tips.body: Tidal output varies through the day, so it is not constant — but the tides are known **years ahead**, so it can be planned around. Wind cannot be predicted beyond a few days, which is a harder problem.

tips.title: Lower impact, not no impact
tips.body: An answer saying wind power has no environmental effect is **weaker** than one naming the visual intrusion, the noise and the birds. Dams flood valleys, barrages alter estuaries, solar farms take land.

tips.title: You need not explain the machinery
tips.body: The spec says descriptions of **how** resources generate electricity are **not required**. Spend the answer on classification, uses, reliability, impact and trends — which is what is marked.

why.matters:
Nothing in a socket was made there. Every joule of electricity was taken from something else, a fuel, the wind, falling water, sunlight, by a machine somewhere else, and the grid has to take exactly as much as is being used at that moment, because electricity is very hard to store.

This topic is about that choice. Each resource is a trade between three things: whether it is there when you flick the switch, whether it will still be there next century, and what using it leaves behind. No resource wins all three, which is why the question does not go away.

examples.title: Why the train has wires and the car has a tank
examples.body:
A vehicle has to carry its energy with it, and a kilogram of petrol holds about 46 MJ against about 0.7 MJ for a kilogram of lithium battery: over sixty times as much. Even allowing for a petrol engine wasting most of that as heat and a motor wasting very little, the tank is still ahead by about 20 to one.

A train escapes the problem because it never leaves its rails. Its energy can be fed to it along the way, from overhead wires. A car cannot, which is why oil is harder to replace on the road than in the power station.

examples.title: A million kettles at half-time
examples.body:
When a big match stops for half-time, a million kettles go on at once. At 2 000 W each that is 2 000 MW, roughly the output of two large power stations, wanted inside a minute. Electricity cannot be kept in a cupboard; something has to start generating at that moment.

That is what *reliable* means here. Hydro-electricity answers in seconds, because the water is already up the hill and a valve is all that opens. Gas takes minutes. Nuclear runs flat out underneath and is not adjusted at all. Wind and the Sun give whatever the weather gives, and half-time is not in the forecast.

visual.alt: A table showing how quickly each resource can be turned up when demand jumps, hydro-electricity in seconds, gas in minutes, nuclear too slowly to adjust, and wind and solar not at all

examples.title: The log and the lump of coal
examples.body:
Both are mostly carbon, both burn, and both send carbon dioxide up the chimney. One is a renewable resource and the other is not, and the definition says why: renewable means **replenished as it is used**.

The log's carbon was in the air about 30 years ago, and a tree planted today will have taken it back in about 30 more. Coal's carbon was in the air about 300 000 000 years ago, and nothing is making any more on a timescale that matters. Burning wood moves carbon round a loop; burning coal opens a store that has been shut for ten million times as long.

steps.title: The resources, and what counts as renewable
steps.body:
**The main energy resources available on Earth** are the ones the specification names, and it is worth knowing the list:

**fossil fuels** — coal, oil and gas — **nuclear fuel**, **bio-fuel**, **wind**, **hydro-electricity**, **geothermal**, **the tides**, **the Sun**, and **water waves**.

**The definition to learn exactly:**

> **A renewable energy resource is one that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used.**

That wording matters. Renewable does **not** mean clean, and it does **not** mean unlimited. It means **replenished as it is used** — the supply is being topped up at the same time as it is drawn on.

**The four non-renewables** are the three **fossil fuels** — coal, oil and gas — and **nuclear fuel**. Everything else on the list is renewable.

**The two that catch people out:**

- **Nuclear fuel is not renewable.** Uranium is mined, and there is a finite amount of it. But it is also **not a fossil fuel** — it is not the remains of living things and it is not burned. So it belongs in neither of the two boxes students expect.
- **Bio-fuel is renewable**, even though it is burned and releases carbon dioxide. It is renewable because the crops are **regrown**, replenishing the supply as it is used. Renewable is about **replenishment**, not about emissions.

Those two together make the point: apply the **definition**, not the feeling.

steps.title: What the resources are used for
steps.body:
The spec asks you to **compare ways that different energy resources are used**, and it names **three uses**:

- **transport**
- **electricity generation**
- **heating**

**Most resources do only one of these well**, and that is the point of the comparison.

**Transport is the hard one.** Almost all transport runs on **oil** — petrol, diesel and kerosene — with some **bio-fuel** blended in, and a growing amount of electricity in cars and trains. Wind, tides and waves cannot power a vehicle directly, because a vehicle has to carry its energy with it. That is why oil has been so hard to replace in transport and comparatively easier to replace in electricity generation.

**Electricity generation is where almost every resource can compete.** All eleven can be used to generate electricity in some form.

**Heating** uses gas and oil heavily in homes, with geothermal and solar contributing where conditions suit.

**A caution that saves time.** The specification says explicitly:

> **Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required.**

So you do **not** need to explain how a turbine works, or how a nuclear reactor produces steam. What you need is to **name** resources, **classify** them, **compare** their uses, discuss **reliability** and **environmental impact**, and explain **patterns and trends**. Knowing what is *not* examinable is worth as much as knowing what is.

steps.title: Reliability
steps.body:
The spec asks you to **understand why some energy resources are more reliable than others**. A **reliable** resource is one that can supply energy **whenever it is needed**, rather than only when conditions allow.

**The reliable ones**, because they can be turned up or down on demand:

- **fossil fuels** — burn more when more is needed
- **nuclear** — steady output, though slow to change
- **bio-fuel** — burned like a fossil fuel
- **geothermal** — constant, where it is available
- **the tides** — not constant, but completely **predictable**: the tide times are known years in advance

**The unreliable ones**, because they depend on conditions outside anyone's control:

- **wind** — no wind, no power; too much wind and the turbines must shut down
- **the Sun** — nothing at night, little in cloud or in winter
- **water waves** — depend on the weather
- **hydro-electricity** — usually reliable, but depends on rainfall, and a drought reduces it

**Tidal is the interesting case**, and a good one to use in an answer. Tidal power is **not constant** — it rises and falls with the tide, and there are times each day when it produces almost nothing. But it is entirely **predictable**, and that is different from being unreliable. A grid operator can plan around something predictable. That distinction — **predictable is not the same as constant** — is the kind of point that separates a good answer from a full one.

**Why reliability matters so much.** Electricity cannot easily be stored in large quantities, so **supply has to match demand minute by minute**. A resource that produces power at the wrong moment is of limited use unless something else can fill the gap. This is the central problem of renewable generation, and it is the reason fossil fuel stations are still kept running.

steps.title: Environmental impact
steps.body:
The spec asks you to **describe the environmental impact arising from the use of different energy resources**. Every resource has one — including the renewables — and saying so is what a balanced answer looks like.

**Fossil fuels.** Burning them releases **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change. Coal and oil also release **sulfur dioxide**, which causes **acid rain**, and burning produces particulates. Extraction damages land, and oil spills damage the sea.

**Nuclear.** No carbon dioxide during generation, and a very small land footprint. But it produces **radioactive waste** that stays dangerous for thousands of years and must be stored securely, and an accident, though rare, can contaminate a large area for a very long time.

**Bio-fuel.** Releases carbon dioxide when burned, though the crops absorbed carbon dioxide while growing. Growing fuel crops uses **land that could grow food**, and clearing land for them can destroy habitat.

**Wind.** No emissions in use. But turbines are **visually intrusive**, make noise, and can kill birds and bats.

**Hydro-electricity.** No emissions in use. But a dam **floods a large valley**, destroying habitat and often displacing people, and it changes the river downstream.

**Tidal.** No emissions. But a tidal barrage alters an **estuary**, which is usually an important habitat for wading birds.

**Solar.** No emissions in use. Manufacturing panels uses energy and materials, and large solar farms take up land.

**Geothermal.** Small impact, but only available where the geology allows.

**The honest summary**: renewables have **lower** impact, not **no** impact. An answer that says wind power has no environmental effect at all is weaker than one that names the visual intrusion and the birds — because it shows you have thought about it rather than sorted the resources into good and bad.

steps.title: Patterns, trends, and why change is slow
steps.body:
The spec asks you to **explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources**. The trend is clear: **away from coal, towards renewables, with gas and nuclear in between**.

**What has driven it:**

- **Concern about climate change**, and international agreements to cut carbon dioxide emissions.
- **Falling costs**: wind and solar have become dramatically cheaper to build.
- **Government policy**: taxes on emissions, subsidies for renewables, and closure dates for coal stations.
- **Improving technology**: larger and more efficient turbines and panels.

**Why the change is not faster**, which is the more interesting half of the question:

- **Reliability.** Wind and solar produce power when conditions allow, not when it is wanted, and electricity is hard to store at scale.
- **Cost and time to build.** A power station or a tidal barrage takes years and very large sums.
- **Existing infrastructure.** Cars, boilers and aircraft already run on fossil fuels, and replacing them all takes decades.
- **Transport** in particular is hard to move off oil, because a vehicle must carry its energy.
- **Political, social, ethical and economic factors.** Jobs depend on existing industries, people object to turbines near their homes, and countries disagree about who should cut emissions first.

**The last point is a spec requirement in its own right**, and it is worth stating carefully:

> **Science has the ability to identify the environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources, but not always the power to deal with them, because of political, social, ethical or economic considerations.**

In other words: **knowing what the problem is, and being able to fix it, are different things.** Scientists can measure carbon dioxide and model the climate; whether a country closes a coal station is decided by governments, voters, industries and economics. A question asking why a known problem has not been solved is asking for exactly this.

**Part A.**

2. Name the four non-renewable resources.

**Part B.**

4. Explain why nuclear fuel is neither renewable nor a fossil fuel.
5. Explain why bio-fuel is renewable even though burning it releases carbon dioxide.
6. Give one environmental impact of wind power and one of hydro-electricity.

8. Explain why transport has been harder to move away from fossil fuels than electricity generation has.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Apply the definition, not the feeling.** *Renewable* means **replenished as it is used**. It does not mean clean, low-carbon or unlimited. That is why **bio-fuel is renewable** despite burning and releasing carbon dioxide, and why **nuclear is not** despite producing no carbon dioxide during generation. Students who sort resources into *good* and *bad* get both of these wrong; students who apply the definition get both right.

**Nuclear fuel fits neither box.** It is **not renewable**, because uranium is mined and finite. It is **not a fossil fuel**, because it is not the remains of living organisms and it is not burned. Being able to say what it is **not** — twice — is a small, precise piece of knowledge that questions do test.

**Predictable is not constant.** Tidal power varies through the day and there are moments when it produces almost nothing, so it is **not constant**. But the tides are known years in advance, so it is **completely predictable** — and a grid operator can plan around what can be predicted. Wind cannot be predicted more than a few days out, which is a different and harder problem. Making this distinction is one of the clearest ways to show you understand reliability rather than having memorised a list.

**Why reliability is the central problem.** Electricity cannot be stored in large quantities, so **supply must match demand minute by minute**. A resource producing power at the wrong moment needs something else to fill the gap — which is why fossil fuel stations are kept available even where renewables supply most of the energy. Every argument about renewable generation comes back to this.

**Renewables have lower impact, not none.** An answer claiming wind power has no environmental effect is **weaker** than one naming the visual intrusion, the noise and the birds, because the second shows judgement. Examiners reward the balanced answer, and the balance is genuine: dams flood valleys, barrages alter estuaries, solar farms take land.

**Transport is the hard case, and there is a physical reason.** A vehicle must **carry its energy with it**, so it needs a resource that is portable and energy-dense. Oil is both. Wind and tides are neither, and cannot be. This is why oil has proved so much harder to displace in transport than in electricity generation, where the resource can stay where it is.

**You do not need to explain the machinery.** The spec says descriptions of **how** resources generate electricity are **not required**. So do not spend the answer on turbines and steam. Spend it on classification, uses, reliability, impact and trends — which is what is actually being marked.

**Science identifies; society decides.** Science can measure emissions and model the climate, but whether a coal station closes depends on jobs, costs, votes and international agreement. A question about why a known problem persists is asking for that distinction, not for more science.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The resources named: **coal, oil, gas** (the fossil fuels), **nuclear fuel**, **bio-fuel**, **wind**, **hydro-electricity**, **geothermal**, **the tides**, **the Sun**, **water waves**.
- **A renewable resource is one being, or able to be, replenished as it is used.**
- Renewable does **not** mean clean, and does **not** mean unlimited.
- The **four non-renewables**: **coal, oil, gas and nuclear fuel**.
- **Nuclear fuel is not renewable and not a fossil fuel.**
- **Bio-fuel is renewable**, because the crops are regrown.
- The three uses: **transport**, **electricity generation**, **heating**.
- **Transport is hardest to change**, because a vehicle must carry its energy with it.
- **Reliable**: fossil fuels, nuclear, bio-fuel, geothermal. **Unreliable**: wind, solar, waves.
- **Tidal is predictable but not constant** — and predictable is enough to plan around.
- Electricity is hard to store, so **supply must match demand minute by minute**.
- Every resource has an environmental impact: fossil fuels give **carbon dioxide** and **acid rain**; nuclear gives **radioactive waste**; hydro **floods valleys**; wind is **visually intrusive**; bio-fuel uses **land that could grow food**.
- **Renewables have lower impact, not none.**
- Trends: away from coal, towards renewables, driven by **climate concern, falling costs and policy**; slowed by **reliability, cost, and existing infrastructure**.
- **Science can identify environmental issues but not always deal with them**, because of **political, social, ethical or economic** considerations.
- **Descriptions of how resources generate electricity are not required.**

questions.prompt: Compare wind power and gas-fired power stations as ways of generating electricity. Refer to renewability, reliability and environmental impact.
questions.solution: Wind is a renewable resource, meaning that it is being replenished as it is used and will not run out, whereas natural gas is a fossil fuel and therefore non-renewable, since the supply is finite and is not replaced on any useful timescale. In terms of reliability, gas is far superior. A gas-fired station can be turned up or down according to demand, so it supplies energy whenever it is needed, and this matters greatly because electricity cannot be stored in large quantities and supply must therefore match demand minute by minute. Wind, by contrast, is unreliable, since it generates only when the wind blows, and it must also shut down when the wind is too strong. Wind output cannot be predicted more than a few days ahead, which is a harder problem for a grid operator than a resource that varies predictably. On environmental impact the comparison reverses. Burning gas releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas contributing to climate change, although it releases less than coal and produces little sulfur dioxide, so it causes little acid rain. Extracting and transporting gas also carries risks. Wind produces no emissions at all in use, but it does not have no impact: turbines are visually intrusive in the landscape, they generate noise, and they can kill birds and bats. Overall, wind is better for emissions and for the long term, while gas is better for reliability, which is why gas stations are often kept available to cover periods when the wind does not blow.

criteria.text: Gives a real impact of wind

questions.modelAnswer:
**Renewability.** Wind is **renewable** — replenished as it is used. Gas is a **fossil fuel**, so **non-renewable**.

**Reliability — gas wins.** A gas station can be **turned up or down on demand**, so it supplies whenever needed. Wind generates only when the wind blows, and must **shut down** if it blows too hard. This matters because **electricity cannot be stored at scale**, so supply must match demand minute by minute — and wind cannot be predicted more than a few days ahead.

**Environmental impact — wind wins, but not completely.**

- **Gas**: releases **carbon dioxide**, contributing to climate change, though less than coal and with little sulfur dioxide, so little acid rain. Extraction and transport carry risks.
- **Wind**: **no emissions in use** — but **not no impact**. Turbines are **visually intrusive**, **noisy**, and **kill birds and bats**.

**The conclusion that earns the top band** is the balanced one: wind is better for emissions and for the long term; gas is better for reliability — which is exactly why gas stations are kept available to cover still days.

questions.prompt: Explain why the change from fossil fuels to renewable resources has been slower than the scientific evidence alone would suggest.
questions.solution: The scientific case for reducing the use of fossil fuels has been clear for some time, since burning them releases carbon dioxide which contributes to climate change, but several factors unconnected with the science have slowed the change. The most important technical obstacle is reliability. Wind and solar generate only when conditions allow rather than when electricity is wanted, and because electricity cannot be stored in large quantities, supply must match demand continuously. This means that conventional stations have to be kept available to cover periods of low output, which reduces the saving that replacing them would otherwise deliver. A second factor is cost and time, since power stations, tidal barrages and new grid connections require very large sums and take many years to build. A third is existing infrastructure, because homes already have gas boilers and roads are full of vehicles with petrol and diesel engines, and replacing all of these takes decades. Transport is the hardest case of all, because a vehicle must carry its energy with it and therefore needs a portable and energy dense fuel, which oil is and wind and tides are not. Beyond these practical considerations lie political, social, ethical and economic ones. Jobs and whole regional economies depend on existing industries, people object to wind turbines being built near their homes, and countries disagree about which of them should reduce emissions first and by how much. This illustrates an important general point, which is that science has the ability to identify environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources but not always the power to deal with them.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The science is clear** — burning fossil fuels releases **carbon dioxide**, which contributes to climate change. What slows the change is mostly not scientific.

**Technical:**

- **Reliability.** Wind and solar generate when conditions allow, not when electricity is wanted, and **electricity cannot be stored at scale**. So conventional stations must be kept available for low-output periods, reducing the saving.
- **Cost and time.** Stations, barrages and grid connections take **years** and very large sums.
- **Existing infrastructure.** Gas boilers and petrol engines are already installed; replacing them takes decades.
- **Transport is hardest**, because a vehicle must **carry its energy** — so it needs a portable, energy-dense fuel. Oil is; wind and tides are not.

**And beyond the technical:** jobs and regional economies depend on existing industries, people object to turbines near their homes, and countries disagree about who should cut emissions first.

**The general point the spec wants**, and the one to finish on: **science has the ability to identify environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources, but not always the power to deal with them**, because of political, social, ethical and economic considerations.

examTechnique.body:
Define renewable as being, or able to be, replenished as it is used, and apply that definition rather than judging by emissions.

Remember that nuclear fuel is neither renewable nor a fossil fuel.

Distinguish a resource being predictable from its being constant, using tidal power as the example.

Give every renewable a genuine environmental impact rather than claiming it has none.

Link reliability to the fact that electricity cannot be stored at scale.

Explain that transport is hardest to change because a vehicle must carry its energy.

Do not describe how a turbine or reactor works, since that is explicitly not required.

For a question about why a known problem persists, refer to political, social, ethical and economic considerations.
examinerErrors: Calling bio-fuel non-renewable because it is burned.
Calling nuclear fuel a fossil fuel.
Treating renewable as meaning clean or unlimited.
Saying tidal power is unreliable, rather than predictable but not constant.
Claiming a renewable resource has no environmental impact at all.
Describing how a power station generates electricity, which is not required.
Answering a question about why change is slow with only scientific reasons.
Forgetting that hydro-electricity depends on rainfall.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer classifies resources by applying the definition rather than by whether they feel clean, so it places bio-fuel and nuclear fuel correctly and can say why each is a special case. It separates predictable from constant and uses tidal power to show the difference. It knows that reliability matters because electricity cannot be stored, and it gives renewables real environmental impacts rather than pretending they have none. It explains why transport is the hardest sector to change with a physical reason rather than a political one, and it finishes a question about slow progress with the distinction the specification itself draws: science can identify the issues, but dealing with them is a political, social, ethical and economic matter.
